Getting started: from results to a Bradley--Terry analysis

Source: vignettes/getting-started.Rmd
getting-started.Rmd

What this package does

BTSBM analyses two kinds of preference data:

  1. Pairwise results: one item wins or loses against another, such as a match in a league.
  2. Rankings: a person places several items from most to least preferred.

This first tutorial uses pairwise results. The ranking tutorial is vignette(“pl-ranking-models”).

A Bradley–Terry (BT) model assigns every player a positive strength. A larger strength means a greater probability of winning against a player with a smaller strength. A BT–SBM additionally lets the data group players with similar strengths into latent tiers.

library(RBBayes)

1. Start with data you can inspect

The toy tennis league is synthetic and intentionally small. wins[i, j] means the number of times player i beat player j. The diagonal is zero because a player does not play themself.

tennis <- tennis_toy(matches_per_pair = 8, seed = 1)
tennis$wins
#>            Ace Baseline Crosscourt Dropshot Elite Forehand
#> Ace          0        5          6        6     5        8
#> Baseline     3        0          3        3     6        6
#> Crosscourt   2        5          0        6     7        7
#> Dropshot     2        5          2        0     4        6
#> Elite        3        2          1        4     0        4
#> Forehand     0        2          1        2     4        0

Before fitting a model, inspect the observed outcomes. Darker cells identify frequent wins by the row player over the column player.

plot_pairwise_outcomes(tennis)

This plot is descriptive: it does not yet account for uncertainty or combine all opponents into one estimate of player strength.

2. Choose a model

Start with a BT–SBM when you think players may form broad tiers rather than a completely reliable order from first to last. Here, the Gnedin prior lets the number of tiers be learned from the data.

model <- bt_sbm_model(
  shape = 4, rate = exp(digamma(4)),
  item_clustering = gnedin_prior(gnedin_hyper = 0.5)
)
model
#> <btsbm_model> Bradley-Terry stochastic block model (BT-SBM), items share block strengths 
#>   strength prior:   lambda_k ~ iid Gamma(shape = 4, rate = 3.512)
#>   item partition:    z ~ Gnedin(gnedin_hyper = 0.5)

shape and rate define the Gamma prior on each block strength \(\lambda_k\). item_clustering is a prior over possible player tiers. You can use finite_partition(max_clusters = 3) when a strict upper limit is scientifically justified.

3. Fit the model

An MCMC fit produces many plausible values rather than one single answer. warmup draws are discarded; the remaining draws represent posterior uncertainty. The short chain below is suitable for a tutorial. Use longer, multiple chains in a real study.

fit <- fit_model(
  tennis,
  model,
  mcmc_control(iter = 400, warmup = 200, seed = 2)
)
fit
#> <btsbm_fit> Bradley-Terry stochastic block model (BT-SBM), items share block strengths 
#>   6 items; 200 retained posterior draws. Use summary() for results.

4. Keep uncertainty in the number of tiers visible

The BT–SBM learns the number of occupied tiers in every MCMC draw. The table reports the posterior probability of each sampled value of \(K\); it is more informative than reporting only the most frequent value.

posterior_K_table(fit)
#>   K draws probability
#> 1 1    18       0.090
#> 2 2   177       0.885
#> 3 3     5       0.025

Concentrated probability on one value means the data resolve the number of tiers clearly. Probability spread across adjacent values means that the broad hierarchy is supported but its precise resolution remains uncertain.

5. Read the tier structure in the observed results

The next figure follows the analysis in Santi and Friel (2026). It reorders the observed win-rate adjacency matrix by a representative posterior partition and, within each tier, by marginal win proportion. The horizontal and vertical boundaries and the coloured side band mark changes between inferred tiers. Mixed colours inside a diagonal block indicate competitive balance within a tier; consistently darker upper-right blocks indicate that stronger tiers tend to defeat weaker ones.

plot_ordered_adjacency(fit)

Observed win rates reordered by the representative BT–SBM partition. Boundary lines and the side band identify inferred tiers.

6. Separate assignment uncertainty from uncertainty in \(K\)

The assignment heatmap conditions on the posterior modal number of tiers by default. This mirrors the paper’s Figure 4: conditioning on \(K\) keeps the question focused on which tier each player belongs to, rather than mixing it with uncertainty about how many tiers exist. Dark cells indicate high posterior membership probability; diffuse rows identify uncertain boundary players.

plot_assignment_probabilities(fit)

Posterior tier-membership probabilities, conditional on the modal number of tiers.

7. Check the sampler before interpreting it

MCMC draws should move around a stable region. Trace plots are a quick screening tool: long trends or a completely stuck trace are reasons to run longer chains or reconsider the model.

plot_mcmc_traces(fit)

mcmc_diagnostics(fit)
#>          quantity  mean       sd      ess       mcse autocorrelation_lag_1
#> 1 n_item_clusters 1.935 0.333664 33.87867 0.05732528             0.6839837

Where to go next

  • Use bt_model() if every item should have its own strength without tiers.
  • Use vignette(“pl-ranking-models”) when the observations are full or top-m rankings rather than wins and losses.
  • Use vignette(“toy-data-gallery”) for additional worked synthetic examples.

Reference

Santi, L. and Friel, N. (2026). The Bradley–Terry stochastic block model. The Annals of Applied Statistics, 20(2), 1766–1787.
